units.passage: If you are willing to give extensions, make sure students know that you are willing to give an extra day or two if they need it. Most students who commit violations do it out of stress.
units.why: "Most students who commit violations do it out of stress" with the advice to offer extensions reduces pressure toward misuse (P99).

units.passage: Citation and Referencing Support: AI tools can guide formatting citations and references according to specific academic styles (e.g., APA, MLA).
units.policy: AI tools can guide formatting citations and references according to specific academic styles such as APA and MLA.
units.why: "AI tools can guide formatting citations and references according to specific academic styles" is a permitted use no type names (citation formatting), so UNCOVERED rather than stretching P91.
units.fit_note: Citation formatting support rather than proofreading or editing prose.
units.uncovered_note: Allows AI to help format citations and references.

units.passage: expressly communicate to students that the access to ChatGPT Edu does not indicate a shift in policy or expectation.
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to expressly communicate to students that the access to ChatGPT Edu does not indicate a shift in policy or expectation.
units.why: Instructors are told to 'expressly communicate to students that the access to ChatGPT Edu does not indicate a shift in policy or expectation'; no type covers the rule that tool provision must not be read as a policy change.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should tell students that university-provided AI tool access does not change the course's AI rules. | Instructors should tell students that the university-provided AI tool does not change the course's AI rule.

units.passage: Transparency: An AI Tool does not provide sufficient explainability or interpretability, such that users of the tool cannot understand why the AI Tool provided particular outputs based on the inputs;
units.why: The Transparency risk (tool "does not provide sufficient explainability or interpretability") is about AI system explainability; no type covers it.
units.uncovered_note: Warns that AI tools may lack explainability or interpretability so users cannot see why outputs were produced.

units.passage: We suggest that generative AI is simply the newest addition to USC’s digital literacy tools.
units.why: Calling generative AI "simply the newest addition to USC's digital literacy tools" frames AI as part of a familiar digital literacy history; no type fits.
units.uncovered_note: Frames generative AI as the latest in a series of digital literacy tools rather than a new kind of problem.

units.passage: Instructors and students share responsibility for communicating about GAI use.
units.why: States a shared-responsibility principle: 'Instructors and students share responsibility for communicating about GAI use'. It spans P09 (instructor) and P78 (student), so neither alone fits.
units.uncovered_note: Principle that instructors and students jointly share responsibility for communicating and clarifying acceptable GAI use. (Coder B coded P78 with fit_note: Shared instructor and student responsibility; the instructor half is also covered in the next unit)

units.passage: We recommend that academic units plan for an ongoing way to continue to address GAI impacts together, select individual topics to review over time, and give progress updates in annual reports.
units.policy: Academic units plan for an ongoing way to continue to address GAI impacts together, select individual topics to review over time, and give progress updates in annual reports.
units.why: Recommends units 'plan for an ongoing way to continue to address GAI impacts', choose topics over time and report 'progress updates in annual reports'. It is about unit-level review and reporting, not revisiting a written policy (P54) or evidence gathering (P55).
units.uncovered_note: Academic units should plan ongoing discussion of GAI impacts and report progress in annual reports.

units.passage: Using Microsoft Copilot, Chat GPT or other AI text generators isn’t necessarily cheating or academically dishonesty.
units.why: "Using Microsoft Copilot, Chat GPT or other AI text generators isn’t necessarily cheating" states that AI use is not automatically misconduct; no type captures that, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: States that using AI text generators is not automatically cheating or an integrity violation.

units.passage: Anecdotally, some students have used AI to write papers for classes (authorized or unauthorized), to draft emails to faculty, to edit papers, and so on.
units.why: The report records that "some students have used AI to write papers for classes (authorized or unauthorized), to draft emails to faculty, to edit papers", a description of observed student uses, not a rule; no type captures reported use patterns.
units.uncovered_note: Anecdotal description of how students are using AI, offered as context.

units.passage: Dean of Students David Strauss suggested that orientation would be a good moment to discuss academic integrity and we agree, along with a first-year course. We furthermore encourage more discussions on the importance of academic integrity on a regular basis through orientations with majors, during advising meetings, during class sessions, and through use of the academic integrity module.
units.why: The report notes the "absence of any discussion about academic integrity at all levels of the institution" and recommends discussing integrity at orientation and in a first-year course; an integrity-education proposal that is not AI-specific and fits no type.
units.fit_note: About academic-integrity education generally, not AI literacy.
units.uncovered_note: Proposes academic-integrity education at orientation, first-year courses and advising, not specific to AI.

units.passage: Currently, if AI is suspected in the writing of an essay, and the student is admissible to WSU, the high school counselor will be contacted to discuss the situation.
units.why: The report states that "if AI is suspected in the writing of an essay, and the student is admissible to WSU, the high school counselor will be contacted"; this is how suspected AI is handled in admissions, which no type covers.
units.uncovered_note: A procedure for suspected AI in admission essays: contact the high school counselor or add a note to the file.

units.passage: Additionally, perhaps proposing a change to the BOG statute that includes authenticity.
units.why: The report proposes "a change to the BOG statute that includes authenticity", amending Board statute; no type covers a statute change. (Final codes after reconciliation: modality may; see resolution_why.)
units.fit_note: Proposes a statutory change on authenticity; names the governing body route.
units.uncovered_note: Proposes amending a Board of Governors statute to address authenticity of applicant work.

units.passage: West Chester University has not yet established a dedicated AI Center.
units.why: "West Chester University has not yet established a dedicated AI Center" is a fact about institutional structure that no type covers, UNCOVERED.
units.fit_note: States no dedicated AI Center exists; not exactly a statement that no policy exists.
units.uncovered_note: States the university has no dedicated AI center and that various offices gather resources instead.

units.passage: These syllabus statements are optional. However, if a statement is used, it must appear in the syllabus exactly as it is listed below (unless otherwise indicated)
units.why: The page says the syllabus statements are optional but verbatim if used; that is a rule on how instructors adopt the Senate text. No type covers optional-but-verbatim adoption, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Senate-approved syllabus statements are optional, but if adopted must be used word for word.

units.passage: To that end, it may be tempting to take a prohibitive classroom policy stance against the use of AI tools, but that is problematic (and potentially unethical).
units.policy: Taking a prohibitive classroom policy stance against the use of AI tools is problematic (and potentially unethical).
units.why: The page warns that 'it may be tempting to take a prohibitive classroom policy stance' but that this 'is problematic (and potentially unethical)'; this advises against blanket bans, which no listed type captures (P03 discourages AI, the opposite direction).
units.fit_note: Advises instructors against prohibiting AI; it does not state an allow-by-default rule for students.
units.uncovered_note: Advises instructors against adopting a blanket prohibitive AI policy because it is problematic and potentially unethical.

units.passage: AI syllabus policies should be being clear, flexible, learner-centered and process-focused.
units.why: The page says 'AI syllabus policies should be being clear, flexible, learner-centered and process-focused'. This is a set of principles for writing a syllabus AI policy addressed to instructors. No type states such principles, and P56 (institution-wide framework) does not fit, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Principles for how to write an AI syllabus statement: clear, flexible, learner-centered and process-focused.

units.passage: If you opt not to use AI tools, when not required, please use the “AI Acknowledgement” to highlight your non-AI approach and/or your reasons for deciding not to use certain tools.
units.why: Students who do not use AI should "highlight your non-AI approach and/or your reasons for deciding not to use certain tools" in the acknowledgement; this extends disclosure to non-use, which no type covers.
units.fit_note: Applies the acknowledgement to students who choose not to use AI.
units.uncovered_note: Students who choose not to use AI use the acknowledgement to describe their non-AI approach or reasons.

units.passage: Academic honesty violations apply to exams, research, course assignments, and other scholarly and/or creative activities. An intent to violate this policy is not required for a violation to occur.
units.why: States that 'An intent to violate this policy is not required for a violation to occur', a liability standard for every academic honesty violation, including the generative-AI one. It is a student-facing rule about when a violation exists; no type covers intent, so UNCOVERED rather than P36.
units.uncovered_note: A violation occurs without any intent to violate the academic honesty policy.

units.passage: If the alleged incident takes place among a group of students, then the Secretary to the Academic Honesty Board may establish one timeline, yet hold each student individually responsible for the violations.
units.why: 'yet hold each student individually responsible for the violations' states that group violations are charged to each student individually. It does not mention AI or set rules for group AI work (P127), so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: In group academic honesty violations each student is held individually responsible.

units.passage: No Students Will Be Allowed to Withdraw From a Course or From the University to Avoid the Consequences of an Academic Honesty Violation
units.why: The heading bars withdrawing "to avoid the consequences of an Academic Honesty Violation"; no type covers closing this escape route, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Students may not withdraw from a course or the university to avoid academic honesty consequences.

units.passage: Students in Violation of Academic Honesty are Not Eligible to Follow the Academic Grievance Procedure
units.why: Students found in violation "are Not Eligible to Follow the Academic Grievance Procedure", which limits routes of challenge; no type fits, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Students found in violation cannot use the academic grievance procedure.

units.passage: AI detection was made available to Western through Turnitin's Simcheck product for a limited time in 2023. That function was discontinued by the vendor and is only available through an advanced product line. Consequently, this leaves Western without an enterprise tool to detect AI writing. ATUS and the CII have been evaluating the new product line by Turnitin and similar tools. In addition, we are continuing our work with faculty committees to understand the university's need for AI detection.
units.why: Western is "without an enterprise tool to detect AI writing" after the vendor dropped the function; this fact about detection capacity fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: The university has no enterprise AI-detection tool and is evaluating options with faculty committees.

units.passage: Because of the evolving nature of AI and AI detection, critics of AI detection have raised concerns of improper AI detection in neurodiverse students or with students with non-standard English. If you have any concerns with a student's work that has been inappropriately flagged for AI usage and you are unsure if they have an accommodation through the DAC, please contact the Disability Access Center
units.why: 'If you have any concerns with a student's work that has been inappropriately flagged for AI usage and you are unsure if they have an accommodation through the DAC, please contact the Disability Access Center' directs instructors to a support office when a flag may be wrong for a neurodiverse student; neither accessibility of AI (P97) nor cost of tools (P51) covers it.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors unsure whether a student wrongly flagged for AI use has an accommodation contact the Disability Access Center.

units.passage: Prior to selecting an AI for a project or task, consult with your department leadership and colleagues.
units.why: "Prior to selecting an AI for a project or task, consult with your department leadership and colleagues" is an employee consult step; no type fits exactly, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Employees should consult department leadership and colleagues before choosing an AI for a task.

units.passage: A good-faith question will never be held against you, and if you ask and follow your professor's written answer, you are fully protected.
units.why: "Asking is always safe. A good-faith question will never be held against you" promises that asking about AI permission carries no penalty, a safe harbor for asking that no existing type covers.
units.uncovered_note: Promises students that asking whether an AI use is allowed (and following the written answer) will never count against them.

units.passage: To make asking safe, this policy establishes a safe harbor. A good-faith question about whether an AI use is permitted will never be held against you.
units.why: "A good-faith question about whether an AI use is permitted will never be held against you" is a safe harbor for asking; no type covers protecting students who ask, so UNCOVERED rather than stretching P10 or P28.
units.uncovered_note: Safe harbor: a good-faith question about whether an AI use is allowed is never held against the student, and a student who follows the instructor's written answer is protected. | Establishes a safe harbor so that a good-faith question about permission is never held against the student.

units.passage: Instructors should answer AI permission questions promptly.
units.why: "Instructors should answer AI permission questions promptly" is a duty on instructors; no type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should respond promptly to student questions about whether an AI use is permitted. | Instructors must respond promptly to students asking whether an AI use is allowed.

units.passage: The safe harbor in Section 5.5 applies in full to any integrity inquiry.
units.why: "The safe harbor in Section 5.5 applies in full to any integrity inquiry" extends protection for good-faith asking into misuse cases; closest P68 (presume good faith).
units.fit_note: Concerns the asking safe harbor in integrity inquiries rather than educative responses to misuse.
units.uncovered_note: The safe harbor for good-faith questions about whether AI use is permitted also applies during an academic integrity inquiry.
